title: Fear, Possessions, Watchfulness, and the Signs of the Time
summary: Before a vast crowd, Jesus warns his disciples against the leaven of the Pharisees and tells them to fear God rather than those who can only kill the body, trusting the Father who counts every hair. Asked to settle an inheritance dispute, he warns against greed with the parable of the rich fool and tells disciples not to worry but to seek God's kingdom and store treasure in heaven. He calls them to be ready for the Son of Man's coming, speaks of the fire and baptism he must undergo and the division he brings, and urges the crowds to read the present time and settle accounts while there is still time.
story:
Chapter 11 ended with the scribes and Pharisees lying in wait to catch Jesus in something he might say. Now, with a crowd of many thousands pressing so close that people trample one another, he turns first to his disciples and prepares them for a hostile world. The chapter moves outward in a series of warnings. Opposition may bring death, but the Father cares for his own. Wealth promises security, but death can come tonight. The master is coming back, but the delay tempts servants to grow careless. Jesus himself faces a baptism of suffering, and his coming will divide even households. The chapter ends with the crowd, who can read the weather but not the time they are living in.

The road to Jerusalem is also the road toward judgment and decision. Much of this teaching has parallels in Matthew, but Luke gathers it into one long address that begins and ends with hypocrisy (verses 1 and 56), and he alone includes the request about the inheritance, the rich fool, the servants whose master waits on them, and the saying about fire and baptism. Chapter 13 continues directly, with news of Galileans killed by Pilate and a call to repent.
historical:
Luke's first readers, probably writing and reading in the decades after Jesus' ministry, knew what it was to be brought before synagogues, rulers, and authorities (verse 11). Acts tells of apostles tried before the Sanhedrin (Acts 4 and 5), of Stephen, whose opponents could not stand up to the Spirit by whom he spoke (Acts 6:10), and of Paul before the Roman governors Felix and Festus and the Herodian king Agrippa II (Acts 24 to 26). Jesus repeats the promise of the Spirit's help in 21:12-15.

The word translated hell in verse 5 is Gehenna, from the Hebrew Ge Hinnom, the Valley of Hinnom, which curves around the south and west of old Jerusalem. Under Ahaz and Manasseh children were burned there as offerings (2 Chronicles 28:3, 33:6) at a site called Topheth, and Josiah defiled it to end the practice (2 Kings 23:10). Jeremiah announced that it would be renamed the Valley of Slaughter (Jeremiah 7:31-32, 19:6). By the time of Jesus the name had become a term for the place of final judgment: 1 Enoch 27 describes an accursed valley for the ungodly, 4 Ezra 7:36 speaks of the furnace of Gehenna, and the Mishnah uses Gehinnom in the same sense (m. Avot 1:5, 5:19-20). The popular idea that the valley was a burning garbage dump goes back only to the medieval commentator David Kimhi, writing around 1200, and has no support in ancient sources or excavation. Luke uses the word only here; Matthew has it seven times.

The coin in verse 6 is the assarion, the Roman as, a small copper coin worth a sixteenth of a denarius, a laborer's daily wage. Matthew 10:29 prices two sparrows at one assarion; Luke has five for two, as though the fifth were thrown in free. The coin in verse 59, the lepton, was the smallest in circulation; two of them made a quadrans (Mark 12:42), the coin named in the parallel at Matthew 5:26.

Inheritance was governed by the Law (Numbers 27:1-11, Deuteronomy 21:17, which gave the firstborn a double portion) and later by the detailed rules of the Mishnah (m. Bava Batra 8 and 9), and people brought disputes to respected teachers for a ruling. Jesus' reply, who appointed me judge or executor between you, echoes the Hebrew's challenge to Moses in Exodus 2:14, which Stephen's speech in Acts 7:27 and 35 applies to Israel's rejection of its deliverers. The Gospel of Thomas, a collection of sayings attributed to Jesus whose date is debated, with most scholars placing it in the second century, has its own versions of the request to divide an inheritance (saying 72), of a rich man who planned to fill his storehouses and died that night (saying 63), of Jesus casting fire on the world (saying 10), and of division within a house of five (saying 16).

The night was divided into three watches in older Israelite reckoning (Judges 7:19 mentions the middle watch) and into four in Roman practice (Mark 13:35), so the second or third watch means the dead middle of the night. In the weather sayings of verses 54 and 55, a cloud rising in the west comes off the Mediterranean with rain (compare 1 Kings 18:44), and a south wind blows hot from the desert. The officer of verse 58 (praktōr) was the court official charged with collecting debts and fines, and imprisonment for unpaid debt was a common practice in the Greek and Roman world (compare Matthew 18:30).
cultural:
Leaven was a lump of fermented dough kept back to raise the next batch, and all of it was cleared from Israelite houses at Passover (Exodus 12:15). It became a natural image for a small, hidden influence that works its way through the whole (1 Corinthians 5:6-8, Galatians 5:9), though Jesus can also use it for the kingdom (13:20-21). Hypocrisy (hupokrisis) comes from the Greek theater, where the hupokritēs was an actor playing a part. Flat roofs were where news was called out, and the inner rooms (tameion, verse 3) were windowless storerooms at the center of a house, the same word Luke uses in verse 24 for the storehouse the ravens do not have.

Sparrows were among the cheapest foods in the market. Hairs of the head being numbered or not falling is a biblical idiom for complete protection (1 Samuel 14:45, 2 Samuel 14:11, Acts 27:34). Ravens were unclean birds under the Law (Leviticus 11:15), yet God feeds them: “Who provides food for the raven when its young cry out to God as they wander about for lack of food?” (Job 38:41, compare Psalm 147:9). The lilies (krinon) are probably wildflowers in general, perhaps the red anemones of the Galilean spring, and dried grass and weeds were used to fire the clay ovens in which bread was baked. Toiling in the field was men's work and spinning thread was women's; the flowers do neither and are clothed more gloriously than Solomon, whose splendor impressed the queen of Sheba (1 Kings 10:4-7).

The rich fool is a landowner whose land produced a bumper crop. In an agrarian village, where most families lived close to subsistence, stored grain was power; the rich man's barns set him in contrast with Joseph, who stored grain in Egypt so that the land would not perish in famine (Genesis 41:35-36). He speaks only to himself, literally to his own soul, with no word to God or to neighbors. His motto, eat, drink, and be merry, echoes Ecclesiastes 8:15 and Isaiah 22:13, and the Jewish wisdom tradition had warned against exactly this: Sirach 11:18-19 describes a man who grows rich by hard work and says he will now enjoy his goods, not knowing that he will soon die and leave them to others, and 1 Enoch 97:8-10 pronounces woe on those who say they have become rich and will now do what they planned. Psalm 49 and Ecclesiastes 2:18-19 make the same point: wealth passes to others.

The servant parables assume a large household run by slaves, with a steward (oikonomos), usually a trusted slave, set over the others to distribute rations. Being dressed for service meant tucking a long robe into the belt, as Israel ate the first Passover ready to leave (Exodus 12:11), and lamps had to be kept trimmed and filled through the night. Thieves in a village with mud-brick walls could dig through a wall rather than force a door, which is the sense of the verb in verse 39. That a master should gird himself and wait on his slaves reverses every expectation (compare 17:7-10), though the Roman festival of Saturnalia licensed a brief, playful exchange of roles. The punishments of verses 46 to 48 reflect the harsh realities of ancient slavery, which Jennifer Glancy (Slavery in Early Christianity, 2002) has argued interpreters too easily read past. A household of five in verse 52 is a typical extended family: father and mother, a son with his wife, and an unmarried daughter, so that the division runs between the generations.
literary:
The chapter is a collection of teaching units joined by catchwords and themes and addressed alternately to the disciples (1-12, 22-53) and to the crowd (13-21, 54-59), with Peter's question in verse 41 turning the second half toward those who lead. It is framed by hypocrisy: the leaven of the Pharisees in verse 1 and the crowd addressed as hypocrites in verse 56. Several words recur and bind the parts together. Do not fear sounds in verses 4, 7, and 32; worry (merimnaō) in verses 11, 22, 25, and 26; the hour in verses 12, 39, 40, and 46; and the idea of being ready. The rich fool prepared goods for himself (verse 20, where the verb is hetoimazō), but the servants must be ready for their master (verse 40), and the servant who did not prepare (verse 47) is punished.

Three arguments from lesser to greater, sparrows, ravens, and lilies, make the case against fear and anxiety, each ending in how much more you are worth to God. The parable of the rich fool (16-21) uses interior monologue, a device Luke's parables use often (15:17-19, 16:3-4, 18:4-5), so that the reader hears the character's heart; the monologue is full of I and my, and then God interrupts it, which is rare in the parables. The first person is broken by the one voice the man never consulted. In the parable of the waiting servants (35-38) the master astonishingly becomes the servant, dressing himself to wait on them at table, and blessings are pronounced on the watchful servants three times (verses 37, 38, and 43). Verses 49 to 53 are a rare first-person statement of Jesus' own mission and inner distress, and verse 53 draws on Micah 7:6, a lament over a society in which households turn against themselves, which Jewish tradition also connected with the time before the Messiah (m. Sotah 9:15). The parallels are spread through Matthew 5, 6, 10, 12, 16, and 24.

outline.t: Fear God, not people; confess the Son of Man
The parable of the rich fool
Do not worry: seek the kingdom

doctrines.note: God feeds the ravens, clothes the lilies, forgets no sparrow, and numbers every hair (verses 6-7, 24-28). His care for his creatures is detailed and personal, and it is the ground for Jesus' command not to fear or worry, since the Father knows what his children need (verse 30).

Life does not consist in the abundance of possessions (verse 15). The rich fool is condemned not for a good harvest or for planning but for storing up for himself without being rich toward God. Disciples are told to give alms and store treasure in heaven, because the heart follows the treasure (verses 33-34). Wealth is neither the proof of God's favor nor evil in itself; it is a test of where the heart rests.

The Son of Man will come at an hour no one expects (verse 40), and the servants who are found ready are blessed. The delay of the master's coming (verse 45) tests faithfulness, and the hope of his return is meant to shape present conduct, especially the conduct of those put in charge of others.

Hidden things will be disclosed (verses 2-3), God has authority to cast into Gehenna (verse 5), the rich fool's life is required of him (verse 20), and servants give account to their returning master. Judgment is proportionate: those who knew more are held to more, and much is required from those given much (verses 47-48).

Blasphemy against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven (verse 10), yet the same Spirit is promised to teach disciples what to say when they stand trial (verse 12). The Spirit who testifies to Jesus is the disciples' helper under pressure, and settled resistance to that testimony shuts a person off from the forgiveness the Spirit brings.

words.note: Hupokrisis, hypocrisy, literally the playing of a part. It occurs six times in the New Testament. In classical Greek the hupokritēs was a stage actor; by the time of the Septuagint and the New Testament the word had come to mean pretense, a gap between the face shown and the heart within. Jesus calls it leaven because it spreads unseen, and he answers it with the certainty that everything hidden will be disclosed (verse 2).

Geenna, Gehenna, the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem. It occurs twelve times in the New Testament, eleven on the lips of Jesus and once in James 3:6, and only here in Luke. It is not the same as Hades, the realm of the dead (10:15, 16:23), but the place of final judgment. Jesus uses it here not to terrify his friends but to put human threats in proportion: persecutors can kill the body, but God holds final authority over life and death.

Pleonexia, greed, literally the desire to have more. It occurs ten times in the New Testament, only here in the Gospels apart from the vice list of Mark 7:22. Paul calls it idolatry (Colossians 3:5), and the Greek moralists treated it as a root of injustice, because the desire for more is always at someone else's expense. Jesus warns against every form of it, since life does not consist in possessions.

Aphrōn, fool, one without sense. It occurs eleven times in the New Testament, twice in Luke (11:40 and here). In the Septuagint it renders the fool of the Psalms and Proverbs, and Psalm 14:1 in Greek uses it of the one who says in his heart that there is no God. The rich fool says nothing against God, but he plans and speaks as if God did not exist, which is the biblical fool's real folly.

Merimnaō, to be anxious, to worry. It occurs 19 times in the New Testament, four times in this chapter and once of Martha (10:41). Jesus does not forbid work, planning, or concern for others, which Paul commends with the same verb (1 Corinthians 12:25, Philippians 2:20); he forbids the anxious grasping that forgets the Father knows what his children need. Verse 29 adds a rarer verb, meteōrizomai, to be up in the air, unsettled, found only here in the New Testament.

Thēsauros, treasure or treasury, the place where valuables are stored. It occurs 17 times in the New Testament, four times in Luke. The rich fool stores up treasure for himself (verse 21, using the related verb); disciples are to store up an inexhaustible treasure in heaven by giving (verse 33). Jewish teaching already spoke of almsgiving as laying up treasure with God (Tobit 4:8-9), and Jesus adds the reason: the heart goes where the treasure is.

Oikonomos, household manager, steward, often a trusted slave put in charge of a master's affairs and fellow servants. It occurs ten times in the New Testament, four in Luke (here and 16:1-8). Paul uses it of apostles as stewards of God's mysteries (1 Corinthians 4:1-2) and of church leaders (Titus 1:7). Peter's question makes the parable apply to leaders among the disciples: those given charge of others will answer for how they feed and treat them.

Baptisma, baptism, immersion. It occurs 19 times in the New Testament, four in Luke. Elsewhere in Luke it names John's baptism (3:3, 7:29, 20:4); here Jesus uses it of his own coming death, an overwhelming like the waters that close over the psalmist (Psalm 69:1-2), as in Mark 10:38-39. The verb for his distress, sunechomai, means to be pressed hard or held in, and it shows the Son's real anguish as he goes toward the cross.

christ:
Jesus speaks here as the Son of Man who will acknowledge or disown people before the angels of God (verses 8-9), the figure of Daniel 7:13-14 who receives the kingdom and in whose kingdom the saints share: “His kingdom will be an everlasting kingdom, and all rulers will serve and obey Him.” (Daniel 7:27). So Jesus can tell his little flock that the Father is pleased to give them the kingdom (verse 32). The one who tells his friends not to fear those who kill the body will himself go to death without fearing them, and the Spirit he promises to his witnesses is the Spirit who filled him.

The picture of the master who, finding his servants awake, dresses himself to wait on them at table is a startling image of the Lord's humility. At the Last Supper Jesus tells his disciples that he is among them as one who serves (22:27), and in John he ties a towel around himself and washes their feet (John 13:4-5). The parable points forward to the messianic banquet, where the returning Lord will serve his own.

Jesus speaks of his death as a baptism he must undergo and of his distress until it is accomplished. John the Baptist had promised that the coming one would baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire (3:16), and here Jesus longs for that fire to be kindled but says his own baptism must come first. The order is the gospel's order: the cross before Pentecost, where tongues as of fire rest on the disciples (Acts 2:3). The division he brings fulfills Simeon's words that the child was a sign to be spoken against, by whom the thoughts of many hearts would be revealed (2:34-35). Finally, the rich fool is the negative image of Christ. The fool stored up everything for himself and lost his soul in a night; Christ, as Paul puts it, though he was rich became poor for our sake, so that we through his poverty might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). To be rich toward God is to be found in him.
interpretation:
The church fathers read the rich fool as a sermon on the social use of wealth. Clement of Alexandria's Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved? (around 200) argued that Jesus demands freedom from the love of possessions rather than their mere disposal, a reading that made room for wealthy Christians who give. Basil of Caesarea preached his homily I Will Tear Down My Barns during the severe Cappadocian famine of about 368 or 369, charging that the grain the rich man hoarded belonged to the hungry, who shared his nature and had a claim on his abundance; Ambrose drew on Basil in his treatise On Naboth. Augustine (Sermon 71) and later Thomas Aquinas (Summa Theologiae II-II q.14) shaped the Western understanding of blasphemy against the Spirit as final impenitence and deliberate resistance to known truth, and Calvin (Institutes 3.3.22) described it as knowingly fighting against the Spirit's light. John Bunyan's Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners (1666) records his long terror that he had committed it, and Bertrand Russell, in his lecture Why I Am Not a Christian (1927), cited the saying as a cause of great misery.

The command to sell possessions (verse 33) has been read literally by monks and friars, by Anabaptist communities that held goods in common, and by movements of voluntary poverty. Thomas Aquinas distinguished precepts binding on all from counsels of perfection such as voluntary poverty, while Luther's attack on monastic vows (1521) and the Reformers' teaching on vocation located faithfulness in ordinary callings. John Wesley's sermon The Use of Money urged Christians to gain, save, and give all they can. Liberation theologians such as Gustavo Gutiérrez (A Theology of Liberation, 1971) made Luke's warnings to the rich central to their reading of the gospel, and Kate Bowler's history of the prosperity gospel (Blessed, 2013) shows how far some modern preaching has moved from this chapter.

On the lilies and the ravens, Søren Kierkegaard wrote three sets of discourses on Matthew's parallel (1847, 1848, and The Lily of the Field and the Bird of the Air, 1849), finding in them teachers of silence, obedience, and joy. The watchfulness parables shaped the church's Advent preaching. Albert Schweitzer read Jesus' ethic as an interim ethic for the short time before an expected end; C. H. Dodd (The Parables of the Kingdom, 1935) read these parables as warnings about the crisis of Jesus' own ministry; and Hans Conzelmann (The Theology of St. Luke, 1954) took the master's delay in verse 45 as evidence that Luke was adjusting the church to a longer wait. Rembrandt's Parable of the Rich Fool (1627, Gemäldegalerie, Berlin) shows an old man studying a coin by candlelight among his ledgers. The Revised Common Lectionary reads the chapter in Year C (Propers 13, 14, and 15).
text:
Most differences between English Bibles here are small. In verse 14 the older Byzantine text has a different word for judge, which does not change the sense. In verse 20 the BSB's ‘your life will be required of you’ renders a plural active verb, literally ‘they are demanding your soul from you’; the plural is often read as a reverent way of speaking of God's action, or of angels sent to take the soul, and the King James Version's ‘thy soul shall be required of thee’ renders it as a passive. In verse 25 the word hēlikia can mean either span of life or stature, and pēchus is a cubit, a forearm's length, so older versions read ‘add one cubit unto his stature’ where most modern versions read ‘add a single hour to his life’. In verse 27 a few witnesses, notably Codex Bezae with some Syriac and Latin manuscripts, read that the lilies ‘neither spin nor weave’ instead of ‘do not labor or spin’.

In verse 31 the earliest manuscripts read ‘His kingdom’, while later ones, followed by the King James Version, read ‘the kingdom of God’, matching Matthew 6:33. In verse 39 later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, add ‘he would have watched, and’ from Matthew 24:43; the earliest witnesses and the editors are divided on it. None of these changes the meaning of the passage.

teach.big: Because the Father who numbers every hair gives his little flock the kingdom, disciples need not fear persecutors, need not hoard or worry, and can live ready for the returning Son of Man, rich toward God.

outline.t: Hypocrisy spreads like leaven and cannot last, because everything hidden will be brought into the light.
Right fear of God casts out the fear of people, and the God to be feared is the Father who forgets no sparrow.
Disciples are called to confess Jesus in public, and the Holy Spirit gives words to those who stand trial for him.
Greed disguises itself as fairness or prudence, but a life stored up for oneself is poor toward God and can be required tonight.
Anxiety is answered not by more possessions but by trust in the Father and by seeking his kingdom, which frees the heart to give.
Readiness for the Lord's return is watchful faithfulness now, and the Lord who returns will serve his servants.
Those entrusted with others are held to a higher account; delay tempts leaders to abuse and self-indulgence.
Jesus goes to his baptism of suffering willingly, and allegiance to him can divide even the closest bonds.
People who read the weather can read the times; the call is to judge rightly and be reconciled before it is too late.

teach.pitfalls:
The rich fool is misused in two opposite directions. Prosperity teaching treats a good harvest as proof of faith and promises that God wants every believer rich; the parable says the harvest came from the land and the fool's error was to keep it for himself. Its mirror image treats all saving, planning, or ownership as sin; Scripture commends Joseph's stored grain and the ant's foresight (Proverbs 6:6-8), and the fool's problem is that he stores up for himself and not toward God. Teachers should also avoid turning verse 33 into a rule imposed on some and ignored by others; Luke shows a range of faithful responses, from Zacchaeus giving half (19:8) to women supporting Jesus from their means (8:3) to Barnabas selling a field (Acts 4:36-37).

The command not to worry is not a rebuke to people with anxiety disorders, nor a prohibition of prudent work; it is an invitation to trust the Father. The blasphemy saying should never be taught in a way that leaves tender consciences terrified, and Gehenna should not be explained by the modern myth of a burning garbage dump. The servant parables use the harsh images of ancient slavery; they do not endorse the beating of slaves but use a familiar world to warn leaders. Verse 53 is not a license to break with family lightly; it describes what may happen when faith in Jesus is opposed, not a goal to pursue.
teach.pastoral: Several groups in the room will feel this chapter sharply. Some live with persistent fear that they have committed the unforgivable sin; tell them plainly that the fear itself shows the Spirit is still at work, and that Peter, who denied Jesus, was restored. Some carry real anxiety about money, work, or illness; Jesus' words are an invitation to trust, not a charge of unbelief, and they sit comfortably alongside medical care and counsel. Some have been estranged from family because of their faith, or have been hurt by families that used faith as a weapon; verse 53 names that grief without celebrating it. People grieving a sudden death may hear the words this very night with pain, and should be reminded that the parable is a warning about greed, not a description of how God takes those we love.

hard.q: What is blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, and why can't it be forgiven?
hard.a:
The objection has been pressed by skeptics and felt by believers. Bertrand Russell, in Why I Am Not a Christian (1927), argued that this saying had caused unspeakable misery, since many sensitive people have feared they committed it, and that no one with proper kindliness would have put such terror into the world. John Bunyan's Grace Abounding (1666) is a first-hand record of exactly that misery. The difficulty is sharpened in Luke, where the saying stands without the explanation Mark gives and seems to contradict the promise that everyone who asks receives (11:10). How can any sin be beyond the reach of a God who forgives?

Christian interpreters have answered from the context. In Mark 3:28-30 and Matthew 12:31-32 the saying follows the charge that Jesus drives out demons by Beelzebul, which Luke reports in 11:15; the sin is seeing the Spirit's work in Jesus and deliberately calling it evil. In Luke it sits between confessing or denying Jesus (verses 8-9) and the Spirit's help for witnesses (verses 11-12), so many read it as settled, final rejection of the Spirit's testimony to Jesus. Speaking against the Son of Man, perhaps while his identity was veiled, can be forgiven, as Peter's denial was (22:61-62). Augustine (Sermon 71) identified the sin as final impenitence, a hardness of heart that refuses forgiveness to the end; Thomas Aquinas (Summa Theologiae II-II q.14) as sin from settled malice that rejects the very means by which sin is removed; and Calvin (Institutes 3.3.22) as knowingly resisting truth the Spirit has made plain. On these readings the sin is unforgivable not because God refuses a penitent sinner but because it refuses repentance. Pastors across traditions have drawn the consequence that someone anxious about having committed it gives evidence that they have not. Skeptics may still judge the saying harsh, but the church has read it as a warning against hardening, not a trap for the tender.

hard.q: Does Jesus require his followers to sell their possessions?
hard.a:
The objection comes from two sides. Critics note that verse 33, sell your possessions and give to the poor, is stated as a command to disciples, and that most Christians ignore it; either Jesus did not mean it or the church does not follow him. Albert Schweitzer argued that such teaching was an interim ethic, radical demands suited only to the short time Jesus expected before the end, and so no longer binding. From another side, some prosperity preachers read Scripture as promising wealth to the faithful, which leaves this chapter unexplained. Jewish tradition, from the Torah's gleaning laws to the Mishnah's rules for charity (tzedakah), valued property, family provision, and ordered generosity rather than renunciation, which sharpens the question of what Jesus intended.

Christians have answered in several ways, and no position should be declared the only faithful one. Some have taken the command literally: monks and friars from Antony of Egypt onward, Anabaptist communities that shared goods in common, and modern movements of voluntary poverty. Thomas Aquinas distinguished precepts binding on all Christians from counsels of perfection, such as poverty, freely taken up by some. Clement of Alexandria, and later Luther, Calvin, and Wesley, read Jesus as demanding inner freedom from wealth and its generous use, so that the command to sell is fulfilled in giving that costs. Liberation theologians read it as a call to solidarity with the poor and to justice in how wealth is gained and shared. Luke itself holds together Zacchaeus, who gives half and repays fourfold (19:8), women who support Jesus from their means (8:3), and believers in Acts who sell property to meet needs (Acts 4:34-37) alongside Mary of Jerusalem, who keeps her house for the church to meet in (Acts 12:12). What all readings share is the text's warning: the heart follows its treasure, and a disciple's use of possessions shows where his heart is.

observe: What three creatures does Jesus point to in verses 6 to 28, and what conclusion does he draw from each?
What does the rich man say to himself in verses 17 to 19, and what does God say to him in verse 20?
What does the master do for the servants he finds awake, and what happens to the servant who says his master is delayed?
interpret: Why does Jesus refuse to settle the inheritance dispute, and what does he see beneath the man's request?
What does it mean to be rich toward God, and how does verse 33 explain it?
What are the fire and the baptism Jesus speaks of in verses 49 and 50, and how do they relate to each other?
apply: Where are you storing up for yourself, and what would it look like to be rich toward God with the same resources this month?
Which worry do you carry most often, and what would change if you believed the Father knows you need these things?
What has been entrusted to you, people, money, or influence, and how would you use it if you expected the master to return tonight?
